messages.author: 3fcf0e009c95d23e
messages.subject: Re: manipulating Effective Strip Width (ESW) values for
parts:
Hi Cooper,

ESW is just the strip width multiplied by the estimated detection
probability, so if you have a lot of variation in ESW it is probably
because your estimated detection functions vary considerably. If there is
no reason to suspect that the true detection function varies between sites,
then the question is why your estimated detection functions vary so much.
I'm guessing its because of small sample sizes. Again, if there is no
reason to suspect that the true detection function varies between
sites, then perhaps you should consider pooling detections across sites to
estimate your detection function. You can still get site-specific density
estimates.

Cheers,

--

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: manipulating Effective Strip Width (ESW) values for
parts:
Cooper, (list)

To augment what Chris said: in terms of modelling detectability, there are 3
options:

1. Fit a global detection function (assumes same detection prob across all
sites). To do this in Distance, you have site as a stratum, and ask for density
estimates and encounter rate by stratum in the model definition | estimate tab,
but detection function global.

2. Fit a separate detection function to each site. To do this you have the same
setup as above, except a different model definition where you tick the box in
model definition | estimate for detection function by stratum.

3. Do multiple covariate distance sampling, where you have site as a covariate
(or some other biologically meaningful variable such as canopy cover). This is
a nice halfway house between 1 and 2. For more on this, see the following
paper, which is available from my web site.
Marques, T.A., L. Thomas, S.G. Fancy and S.T. Buckland. 2007. Improving
estimates of bird density using multiple covariate distance sampling. The Auk
127: 1229-1243.

The above choice is essentially a model selection question, and you can use AIC
to choose among the options. Again, see the above paper, and also the distance
sampling books and Distance manual.

Hope this helps,

- Len
